TinyFish , which provides web infrastructure for AI agents, has published two technical guides addressing these challenges. The first defines a production agentic search architecture , while the second shares lessons from building a deep research system . Together, they examine how an autonomous search agent can plan retrieval, evaluate evidence, handle failures, and manage the boundary between model reasoning and deterministic execution. TL;DR TinyFish introduced its agentic search architecture and key engineering lessons from building deep research systems. Built on four web primitives ( TinySearch, TinyFetch, TinyBrowser, and TinyAgent ), the system operates via a seven-phase control loop around the base model. On OpenBenchmarks, TinyFish achieved a 79.0% completion rate on coding tasks while delivering the lowest median task cost ($0.050) and token footprint, highlighting the importance of rigid control loops, failure-specific retries, and unified reasoning over standalone planners. What is Agentic Search Architecture? Agentic search architecture enables an AI agent to plan retrieval, access sources, evaluate evidence, and adapt its approach as new information becomes available. The model provides reasoning, while the surrounding application manages state, tool execution, evidence handling, runtime policies, and output validation. Together, these components allow an agent to handle incomplete results, recoverable failures, and changing information requirements. TinyFish’s architecture draws foundational concepts from a February 2026 architecture preprint , which decouples reasoning from execution through typed tool interfaces. The paper establishes essential system guardrails, including detailed tracing alongside strict caps on tokens, execution time, overall cost, and tool invocations. How does a production search run work? TinyFish splits a run into 7 phases: Define the task: Turn the goal into an “evidence contract”: required fields, sources, freshness and completion rules. Plan retrieval: Separate independent needs from dependent ones. Dependent queries wait for earlier answers. Pick the first route: Choose a tool based on what the system knows about the evidence. Discover, select, retrieve: Treat search results as candidates until the page content arrives. Evaluate: Label evidence as sufficient, incomplete, conflicting, inaccessible or budget exhausted. Recover or escalate: Revise the query, retry, change sources or change access method. Stop and validate: Return completed, incomplete, failed, cancelled or human review required. Phase 2 addresses a known failure. ChainRAG (ACL 2025) calls it the ‘lost-in-retrieval’ problem, where key entities disappear during multi-hop question decomposition. Phase 6 draws on Search-R1 , which demonstrates how models can learn to generate additional search queries during reasoning when earlier retrieval is insufficient. Across 7 QA datasets, its learned multi-turn search beat RAG baselines by 41% (Qwen2.5-7B) and 20% (Qwen2.5-3B). How should a search agent route tools? Routing should follow the information gap, not a fixed ladder. Weak results need a better query. Conflicting sources need stronger evidence. A heavier tool fixes neither. Retries should be based on the failure type and remain within defined limits. The deep research agent searches, browses, and generates comprehensive, cited reports. Most engineering challenges centered around context management, system orchestration, and product design. Lesson #1: Removing the separate planner Initial iterations used a standalone planner called fresh each time. Only structured state crossed into it. On follow-up queries like “focus only on pricing risks in Southeast Asia,” the agent drifted back to broad market research. TinyFish subsequently moved planning into the orchestrator’s own unified reasoning loop. Lesson #2: Removing subagents: TinyFish initially assigned a separate subagent to each search query, increasing context-switching overhead, latency, and cost. The team later replaced these subagents with tool calls for repeatable tasks such as ranking search results, classifying sources, and extracting evidence. World models built on CADRE run at 20 fps on 1 H100 and react in under 230 ms. The post Kyutai CADRE: Video Autoencoders That Cut World Model Lag Below 230 ms appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Kyutai has released CADRE , open causal diffusion representation autoencoders for interactive world models. The Kyutai CADRE video autoencoder targets one problem: action lag. Many world models borrow autoencoders from text-to-video generators. Those autoencoders pack many frames into one latent, so every action waits. Per the research paper , CADRE world models run at 20 fps on 1 H100 and react within 230 ms. TL;DR Size: 7 autoencoders, each about 476M trained parameters plus a frozen 86M DINOv3 ViT-B/16 . The world model is 1.2B parameters. Video runs at 288×512, 20 fps. Runs on: 1 H100 (bf16, batch 1). Quantized variants: Not disclosed. Performance: CADRE forms most of the latency-quality frontier. It is as fast and better in 42 of 48 comparisons with MIRA, Wan 2.2, Cosmos and LTX-2. Best: Driving FVD of 162.6 (CADRE-2×16×16, 1 step) against 599.7 for Wan 2.2. Worst: Robot manipulation action following (ARR) of 0.45 for CADRE-2×32×32, against 0.85 for Wan 2.2. What is CADRE? CADRE is a family of video autoencoders from Kyutai built for action-conditioned world models. A world model generates in the autoencoder’s latent space. So the autoencoder’s compression sets both cost per frame and action delay. Compression is written τ×s×s. τ is frames per latent, and s is the spatial factor. The research gives the latency as τ/f plus generation and decode time. At τ = 8 and 20 fps, the chunk alone adds 400 ms. Humans notice their own movement lagging beyond about 230 ms. How does CADRE work? The encoder reuses the MIRA recipe. A frozen DINOv3 extracts per-patch features from each frame. One trained 3D convolution then compresses them into a 64-channel latent. Only this bottleneck changes between the 7 members. The decoder is a causal diffusion transformer with 24 blocks. It streams chunk by chunk. Progressive self-distillation teaches it to decode in 1 or 2 steps. This happens in a single training stage, without an adversarial loss. The autoencoders train on 23 public video sources, about 76k hours. The mix spans web, robot, driving and game video. How was CADRE evaluated? Kyutai trained the same 1.2B causal diffusion transformer on each autoencoder. It used 4 environments: robot manipulation (ABC), human manipulation (EgoDex), driving (PhysicalAI AV) and indoor navigation (RealEstate10K). Each model sees 2 s of real video, then generates 4.8 s. Scores cover image quality (FID), motion quality (FVD) and action following (ARR). ARR uses a frozen inverse dynamics probe. An ARR of 1 matches real video. What do the benchmarks show? On one H100, CADRE-2×32×32 reacts in 185 ms and sustains 23.4 fps with 1 decoding step. The Wan 2.2 autoencoder needs 317 ms, LTX-2 492 ms and Cosmos 605 ms. DC-AE is faster at 118 ms but frame-by-frame. The gap is widest with a moving camera. In driving, Wan 2.2 FVD reaches 599.7 and LTX-2 913.3. In indoor navigation, LTX-2 ARR falls to 0.04. Against the retrained MIRA decoder, the 1-step diffusion decoder lowers FVD by 1.4 to 2.5×. What are the 4 findings? Decode by diffusion: at strong compression, perceptual regression blurs, while diffusion samples 1 sharp video. Compress time in the autoencoder: patching inside the world model loses detail. At 8 frames, ARR drops from 0.72 to 0.56. Camera motion decides compression: still cameras tolerate temporal compression. Moving cameras favor fewer frames and coarser spatial tokens. Coarse tokens hurt motion first: in robot manipulation, 32× spatial compression multiplies FVD by 2.4 over 16×. FID barely moves. CADRE uses 1 decoding step. All figures are self-reported by Kyutai. Where does CADRE fall short? CADRE does not win everywhere. In robot manipulation, Cosmos posts an FVD of 39.5 against 47.6 for the best 1-step CADRE. At the fast end, DC-AE beats CADRE-1×48×48 in manipulation. Wan 2.2 also reconstructs held-out video far better, at 35.02 dB PSNR. Kyutai team argues reconstruction does not predict rollouts. Wan 2.2 ranks last on indoor rollout FVD. Long latents leave visible seams between chunks. At τ = 8, boundary excess reaches 1.6 to 1.8 across environments. CADRE-4×24×24 is an outlier in navigation, with FVD 403 in driving. Each world model covers one environment at 288×512. Whether findings transfer to generalist models remains open. How can developers use CADRE? The code is MIT licensed. Weights on Hugging Face are CC BY-NC 4.0, so commercial use is excluded. The release covers 7 autoencoders, 4 longer-trained multi-resolution versions and 4 world models on CADRE-2×16×16. A live demo lets you drive them by keyboard. Key Takeaways 7 open autoencoders, one bottleneck apart, isolate compression as the only variable. World models on CADRE run at 20 fps on 1 H100, under 230 ms lag. Driving FVD drops to 162.6, against 599.7 for Wan 2.2. Still cameras favor temporal compression; moving cameras favor spatial compression. Weights are non-commercial (CC BY-NC 4.0); code is MIT.
